objective: PATTERN-3D-20261025-001 showed that counting laws whose long edge is a function of the short edges are groupoid laws, so their counts are numbers of homomorphisms from the fundamental group into finite groups. Ask where such counting becomes hard. Known: polynomial for abelian groups; polynomial for class-2 nilpotent groups on closed triangulated manifolds when |H2(M; Z(G))| is bounded (Samperton and Weiss, 2026); #P-complete for non-abelian simple groups (Kuperberg and Samperton, 2018). Samperton and Weiss name the symmetric group on three letters and the dihedral group of order 16 as the most interesting open cases. Test whether counting homomorphisms into them is #P-hard, using handlebodies with thickened tori attached along curves drawn from a planar graph, and their doubles for closed manifolds. Hypothesis under test: the counts are spin models on the graph whose repeated edges, by interpolation, recover numbers of proper colourings. Standalone value: the complexity of the smallest non-abelian three-dimensional counting laws.
status: Complete 2026-10-25: where counting in three dimensions becomes hard. Counting homomorphisms from 3-manifold groups into S3 is #P-hard: with boundary via fin handlebodies over planar graphs (twice the 3-colourings), and on closed manifolds via their doubles, which count pairs of colourings (2 P(G,9)/3^|V|); the same holds for every dihedral group whose order is not a power of 2 at least 16, Q8 and A4, and for the class-2 groups among them it shows the bounded-H2 hypothesis of Samperton and Weiss is necessary. The order-16 dihedral group remains open. Next: the full dichotomy (3/3); execution deferred to the owner.
title: Where counting in three dimensions becomes hard
